analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal agencies from clarifying which waterways are protected by the Clean Water Act.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 40 Senate Republicans, never got a hearing or vote — it died in the Senate committee it was referred to in March 2012.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2011-2012, the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers proposed guidance — informal instructions to their own staff — clarifying which streams, wetlands, and other waters count as 'waters of the United States' under the Clean Water Act. After Supreme Court rulings, millions of acres of wetlands and many upstream streams sat in a gray zone where federal pollution protections were uncertain. This bill would have legally banned the agencies from finalizing that guidance or using anything similar, and allowed any rule based on it to be thrown out in court. It never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been land developers, homebuilders, agricultural operations, mining and energy companies, and other businesses that fill wetlands or discharge into streams — activities that would face less federal permitting and pollution oversight if fewer waters counted as protected. Landowners who wanted fewer federal restrictions on their property would also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, agriculture, mining and energy firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the Army Secretary and EPA Administrator from finalizing the 2011 draft guidance on identifying waters protected by the Clean Water Act, and from using that guidance — or anything substantially similar — for any Clean Water Act decision or rulemaking [S2][S3].
It would make any rule based on the guidance subject to being vacated by courts, giving regulated businesses a ready-made legal challenge [S3].

By freezing the existing narrower interpretation of which waters are protected, the bill would preserve the status quo that left many streams and wetlands without clear federal pollution protections, reducing permitting burdens for land-disturbing industries [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on everyone downstream of unprotected waters: the EPA and Army Corps would have had to continue treating many streams and wetlands as outside the Clean Water Act, allowing pollution discharges and wetland filling without federal permits. Communities relying on those waters for drinking water, fishing, and recreation would bear the risk, and downstream states could not rely on upstream federal enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The core objection supporters raised was that the guidance would expand federal jurisdiction over private land and small waters — including farm ponds, drainage ditches, and isolated wetlands — without a new act of Congress, subjecting landowners to federal permitting requirements by administrative instruction [S2][S3].

An honest supporter of the guidance would acknowledge a real cost: after the Supreme Court's split decision in Rapanos v. United States, the jurisdictional gray zone creates genuine uncertainty for property owners, and the path the bill blocked left that ambiguity unresolved until a formal rulemaking years later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered regulated industries lower compliance costs and less permitting friction, but by locking agencies out of clarifying Clean Water Act coverage — and voiding any future rule built on the guidance — it would have left millions of acres of streams and wetlands without clear pollution protections. The benefit flowed mainly to businesses that fill or discharge into waters; the cost fell on the public's water supply with no offsetting protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late March 2012 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died there when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barrasso and 30 original Republican cosponsors introduced the bill on March 28, 2012 [S3].
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, the only action recorded in its history [S1][S5].

It attracted 39 cosponsors, all Republicans, but the committee — controlled at the time by Democrats — never held a hearing or markup, and no further action appears before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA and Army Corps kept authority to determine the scope of Clean Water Act jurisdiction, and the businesses that would have gained a near-automatic court challenge to any jurisdictional rule did not get it. People who depend on federally protected waters were spared a statutory freeze of the narrower interpretation.

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 39 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Minority Leader Sen. McConnell and senior committee members, giving it full Republican Senate support.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors and the sponsor were Republicans, with no Democratic support; the Democratic-led committee never advanced it.

industries.note: Developers filling wetlands or building near streams would face less federal permitting and pollution oversight if fewer waters counted as protected waters of the United States. The public bears the resulting loss of wetland and stream protections.

Farmers argued the guidance could subject drainage ditches, ponds, and adjacent wetlands to federal permitting without new legislation. Blocking it preserved the narrower status quo for agricultural land use.

Mining and energy projects that discharge into or disturb upstream streams would face fewer jurisdictional hurdles. Less federal oversight of those discharges shifts pollution risk onto downstream water users.

industries.industry: EPA and Army Corps of Engineers
industries.note: The bill would strip both agencies of authority to define the reach of the Clean Water Act through guidance or rulemaking built on it, and expose any such rule to automatic vacatur.
